newsitem.title: USA: Grains soar on hot, dry weather, oil falls.
newsitem.headline: Grains soar on hot, dry weather, oil falls.

text.p: Corn and soybean prices soared on Monday on fears that hot, dry weather in the Midwest will hurt crop growth as the plants enter a key growth stage.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn and soybean prices both jumped their daily allowable trading limits from the opening bell and stayed there most of the session.
"The key is that we seem to have missed the rain and it looks like it's going to be warm through Wednesday and Thursday," said Jerry Gidel, a grain analyst with Dean Witter.
Corn for post-harvest delivery in December closed up the 12-cent a bushel trading limit at $2.49, with July delivery corn up 10-3/4 cents to close at $2.62-1/4.

Soybeans for post-harvest delivery in November closed 28 cents a bushel higher at $6.21-3/4, just off the 30-cent daily limit. July soybeans, now in a cash delivery period and not subject to limits, closed 33-1/2 cents higher at $8.19.

Most analysts continue to expect bumper crops this fall, a view that has pushed grain prices lower since May. Conditions of Midwest crops generally continue to be excellent, according to Agriculture Department reports issued late Monday.

As of Sunday, 73 percent of the U.S. corn crop was rated in good to excellent condition, compared to 75 percent a week earlier. Soybeans were rated 66 percent at that level, compared to 68 percent a week earlier.

However, many forecasters said hot, dry conditions are expected to continue for at least five days in pockets of Illinois, Iowa and Missouri, which may stress the corn crop during its pollination period.
Smith Barney meteorologist Jon Davis wrote in a daily report issued Monday: "The bottom line is that the central and eastern Midwest is in a drier than normal pattern during the next 10 days."
Dave Armstrong, an analyst for ABN Amro/Chicago Corp, said, "The fact is, we didn't get the central Illinois rain and the perception is there may be some kind of a change in the pattern."
Buoyed by weather nerves in other grains, wheat prices also rose on concern that dryness may hurt spring-planted wheat. July wheat rose 7 cents to close at $3.29 a bushel.

At the New York Mercantile Exchange, crude oil prices led other energy markets lower on news that Iraq and the United Nations had agreed to Iraq's new aid distribution plan, moving Iraq a step closer to resuming oil sales.

August crude settled off 34 cents at $18.99 a barrel. Refined products tracked crude lower, with August heating oil ending down 0.68 cent at 51.67 cents a gallon and August gasoline finishing down 0.91 cent a gallon at 58.35 cents.

Iraq needed to complete an aid distribution plan before resuming oil sales under a deal with the U.N. that enables Iraq to sell $2 billion of oil every six months on a renewable basis to buy food, medicine and humanitarian aid. The second six-month period was to start June 8.

The U.N. coordinator in Baghdad, Staffan De Mistura, said on Monday that discussions about the aid plan had been completed and the plan would be submitted to U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan for approval by next Monday.

"When the Iraq news hit this morning, it came as a big surprise. People had thought there would be more delays in the daal, so the news was a real slam dunk for prices," said Warren Tashnek, president at Fimat USA Futures in Houston.

"The marketplace realizes that Iraq may have to sell a lot of oil in a shorter period of time, which just means the market will have to suddenly absorb a lot more crude," said Scott Ryll, a dealer and analyst with GSC Energy in Atlanta.
Adding to the bearish supply news, Germany said on Monday it would start selling its strategic crude oil reserves in stages in early August.

Last week, Bonn said it planned to sell $230 million of crude in 1997 to narrow its budget deficit, with more sales seen in 1998. The sales will add about 75,000 barrels per day in oil supplies to an already glutted marketplace.
